choice.open_phrase: greater area than that of any country in Europe
choice.why_both: In English, 'greater than any X' usually means 'greater than all X' (a free-choice universal), but SQL's '> ANY' and a literal existential reading mean 'greater than at least one', so either reading is reasonable.

original: Which cities are in European countries where English is not the official language?
explicit: Start from each `country` record; combine it with each `city` record for which Country Code (`city.CountryCode`) equals Code (`country.Code`) (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which all of the following hold: [1] continent (`country.Continent`) equals 'Europe' (compared as text, character by character); [2] Name (`country.Name`) is none of the values returned by [start from each `country` record; combine it with each `countrylanguage` record for which Code (`country.Code`) equals Country Code (`countrylanguage.CountryCode`) (compared as text, character by character), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); keep only the records for which all of the following hold: [1] language is official (`countrylanguage.IsOfficial`) equals 'T' (compared as text, character by character); [2] language (`countrylanguage.Language`) equals 'English' (compared as text, character by character) [end]; for each kept record, return (1) Name (`country.Name`)] (when [the bracketed query] returns no rows it is true, even for a missing value; otherwise(false when it equals one of them; undetermined when it is missing, or when it equals none of them and one of them is missing; otherwise true) [end]; for each kept record, return (1) city name (`city.Name`); remove duplicate result rows.
gold_sql: SELECT DISTINCT T2.Name FROM country AS T1 JOIN city AS T2 ON T2.CountryCode  =  T1.Code WHERE T1.Continent  =  'Europe' AND T1.Name NOT IN (SELECT T3.Name FROM country AS T3 JOIN countrylanguage AS T4 ON T3.Code  =  T4.CountryCode WHERE T4.IsOfficial  =  'T' AND T4.Language  =  'English')

original: What are the different continents and the total popuation and average life expectancy corresponding to each, for continents that have an average life expectancy less than 72?
explicit: Start from each `country` record; group the kept records by continent (`country.Continent`); each group gives one result row; keep only the groups for which the average of life expectancy at birth (`country.LifeExpectancy`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none) is less than 72; for each result row, return (1) the sum of country population (`country.Population`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (2) the average of life expectancy at birth (`country.LifeExpectancy`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none); (3) continent (`country.Continent`).
gold_sql: SELECT sum(Population) ,  avg(LifeExpectancy) ,  Continent FROM country GROUP BY Continent HAVING avg(LifeExpectancy)  <  72
decision: Whether countries with a missing (NULL) life expectancy still count toward a continent's total population

readings.reading: Total population sums every country on the continent, including countries with no recorded life expectancy. The average life expectancy covers only the countries that have a value.
readings.sql: SELECT sum(Population) ,  avg(LifeExpectancy) ,  Continent FROM country GROUP BY Continent HAVING avg(LifeExpectancy)  <  72

readings.reading: Use only countries that have a recorded life expectancy, so countries with no life expectancy are left out of both the total population and the average.
readings.sql: SELECT sum(Population) ,  avg(LifeExpectancy) ,  Continent FROM country WHERE LifeExpectancy IS NOT NULL GROUP BY Continent HAVING avg(LifeExpectancy)  <  72

other_readings: Count countries with no recorded life expectancy as 0 in the average (COALESCE to 0), which lowers the average and can change which continents fall below 72.
Compute the total population from the city table (sum of city populations) rather than country.Population.
Treat missing life expectancy as 0 in the average, which pulls the averages down and changes which continents pass the < 72 filter.
Use a population-weighted average life expectancy instead of a simple mean across countries.

inspection.difference: The submission adds `WHERE LifeExpectancy IS NOT NULL`, which removes countries with no life expectancy from the population sum. Oceania becomes 30377000 instead of 30401150, and South America 345778000 instead of 345780000. The submission also puts columns in the order `Continent, SUM, AVG` while the gold uses `sum, avg, Continent`.
inspection.question_gap: partly — the question doesn't ask to drop null-life-expectancy countries from the total population, but it also doesn't fix the column order.
inspection.supplied: the sum of country population (`country.Population`) in the group (missing values ignored...) — with no filter on LifeExpectancy before grouping; output order (1) sum, (2) average, (3) continent

original: What is the lowest grade of students who do not have any friends?
explicit: Start from each `Highschooler` record; keep only the records for which ID (`Highschooler.ID`) is none of the values returned by [start from each `Friend` record; combine it with each `Highschooler` record for which student id (`Friend.student_id`) equals ID (`Highschooler.ID`), one combined record per match (a record without a match is dropped); for each kept record, return (1) student id (`Friend.student_id`)] (when [the bracketed query] returns no rows it is true, even for a missing value; otherwise(false when it equals one of them; undetermined when it is missing, or when it equals none of them and one of them is missing; otherwise true); all kept records form one group, which gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) the smallest school grade level (`Highschooler.grade`) in the group (missing values ignored; missing when there are none).
gold_sql: SELECT min(grade) FROM Highschooler WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT T1.student_id FROM Friend AS T1 JOIN Highschooler AS T2 ON T1.student_id  =  T2.id)
decision: Whether a student who appears in Friend only as friend_id (someone else lists them as a friend) counts as having a friend

readings.reading: A student has no friends if they never appear as student_id in the Friend table. Being listed as someone else's friend_id does not count.
readings.sql: SELECT min(grade) FROM Highschooler WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT T1.student_id FROM Friend AS T1 JOIN Highschooler AS T2 ON T1.student_id  =  T2.id)

readings.reading: A student has no friends only if they appear nowhere in the Friend table, as neither student_id nor friend_id. Friendship is treated as two-way.
readings.sql: SELECT min(grade) FROM Highschooler WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT T1.student_id FROM Friend AS T1 JOIN Highschooler AS T2 ON T1.student_id  =  T2.id) AND id NOT IN (SELECT T1.friend_id FROM Friend AS T1)

other_readings: A student has no friends if they never appear as friend_id (no one lists them as a friend), whatever their own student_id rows say.
Student has no friends if they appear only as friend_id (not as student_id) is the complement of R2, but it is not a distinct reading of 'no friends'.

The lowest grade could be read as the minimum grade value across friendless students (a single number), versus the grade of the student(s) at the lowest level of an ordering; the minimum-value reading is the natural one.
Friendless could be read as having no friends among other students only, ignoring self-friendships where student_id equals friend_id.

inspection.difference: Both original repeats treated friendship as two-way and also excluded IDs that appear as friend_id: "AND ID NOT IN (SELECT DISTINCT friend_id FROM Friend)" in one, "UNION SELECT DISTINCT friend_id" in the other. That left no students, so the result was [[None]]. The gold excludes only Friend.student_id and returns [[10]].
inspection.question_gap: partly -- 'do not have any friends' does not say whether appearing only as friend_id counts as having a friend, and the two readings give different answers on this data.
inspection.supplied: ID (`Highschooler.ID`) is none of the values returned by [... return (1) student id (`Friend.student_id`)]

uses a negated existence phrase ('do not have any') without saying how a missing value behaves inside the exclusion

However, under that reading no student is friendless and the result is NULL. That clashes with the question's assumption that friendless students exist, which favours the directed reading in the gold.

original: Please show the most common citizenship of singers.
explicit: Start from each `singer` record; group the kept records by country of citizenship (`singer.Citizenship`); each group gives one result row; for each result row, return (1) country of citizenship (`singer.Citizenship`); order the result rows by the number of records in the group descending (missing last); keep only the first 1 rows.
